title: What are Japanese stragglers?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss Japanese stragglers, Imperial Japanese soldiers who kept fighting World War II after the war ended. They cover the kamikaze suicide pilots and the bushido code that supported them, Japanese soldiers' refusal to surrender in Pacific island battles, and the Japanese holdouts Hiroo Onoda (Lieutenant Onoda) on Lubang Island, Shoichi Yokoi found on Guam in 1972, and the Japanese soldier who settled in Ukraine and the cannibalism-linked group with the woman Kazuko. They describe Suzuki's search for Onoda, Onoda's surrender after a formal order, and pop-culture references including a Gilligan's Island episode. The episode closes with a listener email from Natalie about whether someone can be framed for murder.

segments.title: Opening banter and WWII kamikaze setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then Josh introduces how Japan's aging air force in late World War II led to the kamikaze program under Vice Admiral Onishi Takijiro, with pilots flying bomb-laden planes into ships.
topics: Japanese air force World War II

segments.title: Psychology of suicide attacks and bushido
segments.summary: The hosts discuss suicide bombing and a study suggesting mosque attendance, not daily prayer, correlated with support for it. They tie kamikaze motivation to the samurai code of bushido, including the idea that honor comes from death and disgrace from surrender.

segments.title: Kamikaze impact and Japanese reluctance to surrender
segments.summary: They describe the first kamikaze attacks, including the sinking of the USS St. Lo, and the Battle of Okinawa. They note that the bushido perversion extended beyond pilots, with very few Japanese soldiers surrendering in Pacific island battles.

segments.title: Pacific islands, Philippines, and stragglers hiding in jungles
segments.summary: The islands became strategic focal points for both sides. The Japanese set up a puppet regime in the Philippines, and after Allied liberation Filipino search parties hunted hidden Japanese soldiers. Some soldiers hid in mountains and jungles as stragglers.

segments.title: Lone holdouts: Soldier in Russia-area island, Ukrainian settler, and the cannibalism group
segments.summary: A soldier who kept defending an island off eastern Russia until 1959 later settled in Ukraine and started a family. Another group of about thirty survivors, including one woman named Kazuko, lived on a mountain for years, with violence and disappearances among them.

segments.title: Shoichi Yokoi found on Guam
segments.summary: Shoichi Yokoi was discovered fishing on a Guam riverbank in 1972 wearing burlap pants and bark shirt. He said he stayed out of shame about surrendering, and he was met with national embarrassment.

segments.title: Hiroo Onoda on Lubang Island
segments.summary: Lieutenant Hiroo Onoda and four other saboteurs stayed on Lubang Island after the Allied invasion and kept fighting as guerrillas. Leaflets and loudspeaker messages that the war was over failed to convince them. Onoda's men died one by one, and he continued raids, including on a police station, into the 1970s.

segments.title: Suzuki's search and Onoda's surrender
segments.summary: Naoya Suzuki, a Japanese dropout, found Onoda in 1974 and they became friends. Onoda would only surrender after a direct order from his former commanding officer, which was delivered in Lubang. Onoda later was pardoned by Ferdinand Marcos and returned home as a national hero.

segments.title: Pop culture and unverified holdout reports
segments.summary: The hosts mention a Gilligan's Island episode featuring a Japanese holdout character played by an Italian actor, and note that reported later holdout discoveries were never substantiated.

segments.title: Listener mail: framing for murder
segments.summary: Listener Natalie asks whether someone can be framed for murder after her husband Paul had two accidents. The hosts respond that framing usually involves a murder committed by someone else, not a staged self-murder.
